title: Acknowledge before you disagree
goal: Restate a colleague's concern fairly before explaining a different view.
prompt: A colleague says: 'I don't think we should launch next month. Testing has been rushed, and the last time we hurried, the support team was flooded with complaints.' You would prefer to launch on time. In about 60 seconds, first restate their concern and the worry behind it, then give your view and suggest one way to reduce the risk they raised.

provenance.notes: From app seed tech_listening (disagreement practice with a summary before replying); original scenario; reviewer to add sourceVideoId/sourceUrl/timestamps and verify wording

title: Calm an unhappy customer
goal: Show a frustrated customer you understood what happened and how they feel before offering a fix.
prompt: A customer says: 'This is the second time my order has arrived damaged, and nobody has called me back.' Reply in about 45 seconds. Start by reflecting what happened and how they feel, without excuses. Then say sorry for the right thing and explain exactly what you will do next and by when.

provenance.notes: From app seed tech_listening; original scenario; reviewer to add sourceVideoId/sourceUrl/timestamps and verify wording

title: Bottom line first for a busy manager
goal: Give a 30-second update that opens with the outcome and the decision you need.
prompt: Your project will finish two weeks late, but it will now cost less than planned. Give a 30-second update to a senior manager who has little time and cares about results. Open with the outcome and the decision you need from them, add one supporting fact, and stop.

title: Evidence first for a detail-minded colleague

prompt: Your project will finish two weeks late but under budget. Explain this in about 45 seconds to an analyst who likes facts and proof. Lead with the key numbers and where they come from, then explain the cause, and close with the next step and how you will track it.

title: People first for a team-minded listener
goal: Pitch a change by opening with how it affects people and inviting their view.
prompt: You want to move your team's weekly meeting from Friday afternoon to Tuesday morning. Pitch the idea in about 45 seconds to a teammate who cares most about how changes affect people. Start with how it helps the team, acknowledge who might find it harder, and finish by asking for their view.

title: Crisp endings in a team update
goal: Read a short work update at normal speed with every word ending clearly finished.
prompt: Read this update as if you were opening a team meeting. Use your everyday speaking speed, not the slow drill pace, but keep the endings crisp: listen for the t in last, the d in signed and the k in week.
referenceText: Good morning, everyone. The client signed the contract last night, so the project starts next week. Our first task is to fix the date for the kick-off and check the budget. Please send any questions to Mark by Friday at five, and thanks again for all the hard work.

provenance.notes: From app seed tech_articulation (normal-speed transfer step); reference text written from scratch; reviewer to add sourceVideoId/sourceUrl/timestamps and verify wording

title: Pick up a thread
goal: Reply to a new acquaintance by following a detail they mentioned, adding your own context and asking an open follow-up.
prompt: A new colleague says to you: I just moved here from the coast, and I am still trying to find somewhere decent for coffee. Reply as you would in person. Pick up one thread from what they said, share a short related thought of your own, and ask an open follow-up question. Then pick up their other thread and do the same again.

title: Explain Your Work to a Newcomer
goal: Explain something from your job or studies in about 90 seconds so that someone outside your field could follow it.
prompt: Explain one thing from your work or studies to a friend who has never worked in your field. Start with something they already know, use one everyday comparison, and explain or avoid every acronym. Say why it matters, either to them or to the people it helps, and finish with a single sentence that sums it up. Aim for about ninety seconds.

title: Technical Proposal for a Busy Manager
goal: Pitch a technical change to a non-specialist manager in about a minute, leading with what it means for the team.
prompt: You want approval for a technical change, such as automating a report your team builds by hand or moving shared files into one system. Your manager is not a specialist and has one minute. Say what the change is in plain words, compare it to something familiar, explain what the team gains in time, cost or fewer errors, and close with one sentence that sums up your request.

title: Think in silence under pressure
goal: Answer an unexpected question and take your thinking time silently instead of filling it with sounds.
prompt: A manager stops you in the corridor and asks: 'If you could change one thing about how our team works, what would it be?' Answer in about 45 to 60 seconds. You have almost no time to prepare, so you will need thinking time as you go. Take it as a silent pause with your lips closed, not as um, uh or you know. A clear pause before your first sentence is fine.

title: Explain Something Technical to a Beginner
goal: Make a technical topic easy to follow for someone with no background, using a familiar comparison and no jargon.
prompt: Pick something technical you understand well, such as how a phone knows where you are, how contactless payment works, or a detailed hobby of yours. Explain it in about 90 seconds to a relative who has never thought about it. Start from something they already know, compare it to an everyday activity, describe what it does for them, leave out jargon, and finish by repeating the one idea you want them to remember.

title: Keep Subject and Verb in Agreement
goal: Match each verb to its real subject, even when a long phrase sits between them.
prompt: Talk for about 45 seconds about your strengths and how other people see you. Include at least three sentences where a longer phrase comes between the subject and the verb, such as The list of tasks on my desk is getting shorter, or Each of my teammates has a different way of working. Make the verb agree with the main subject, not with the noun closest to it.

provenance.notes: From app seed gram_sva (CurriculumCatalog.grammarLessons). Re-expressed in original wording with new example sentences. General grammar practice, not tied to a channel technique. Reviewer to verify wording.

title: Link Ideas With Although, Because and As a Result
goal: Join cause, contrast and result into smooth, longer sentences instead of short, separate ones.
prompt: Describe a challenge you faced and how you dealt with it, in about 30 to 45 seconds. Instead of short, separate sentences, join your ideas: use although to show a contrast, because to give a reason, and as a result to show what changed. For example: Although the order arrived late, we kept the customer because we called them first, and as a result they ordered again.

provenance.notes: From app seed gram_complex (CurriculumCatalog.grammarLessons). Re-expressed in original wording with a new example sentence. General grammar practice, not tied to a channel technique. Reviewer to verify wording.

title: Propose Ideas With the Second Conditional
goal: Suggest a change tactfully with sentences such as If we tried this, we would see that.
prompt: Suggest one improvement to the way your team, class or household does something. Speak for about 45 seconds and use at least two sentences built as If we plus a past-tense verb, followed by we would plus a base verb. For example: If we shared the agenda a day early, we would finish our meetings faster.

provenance.notes: From app seed gram_conditionals (CurriculumCatalog.grammarLessons). Re-expressed in original wording with a new example sentence. General grammar practice, not tied to a channel technique. Reviewer to verify wording.

title: One-Minute Opinion With PREP

prompt: Is working from home better than working in an office for getting focused work done? Give your view in under a minute. Say your answer in the first sentence, give one reason, support it with one specific example from your own experience or from someone you know, and finish by stating your view again in fresh words.

title: Falling Statements, Rising Questions
goal: End statements with a falling pitch so they sound certain, and lift your pitch on genuine yes-or-no questions.
prompt: Read the three statements with your voice stepping down on the final word, so each one sounds finished and sure. Then let your pitch rise gently at the end of the two questions, which invites the listener to answer. Avoid lifting your voice at the end of the statements, as that can make them sound unsure.
referenceText: The report is ready. The budget has been approved. We start on Monday. Does anyone have a question about the plan? Is Monday still good for everyone?

provenance.notes: From app seed pron_intonation (CurriculumCatalog.pronunciationDrills). Reference text is newly written; the seed sentence was not reused. Reviewer to verify wording.

title: Repeat a Point-First Opening
goal: Copy a model that states its point with a firm, falling voice, pauses, then moves into an example.

title: Two-Minute Proposal for a Change
goal: Pitch one change with a gripping opening, three clear supporting points and a firm, settled close.
prompt: Prepare a two-minute proposal for one habit, tool or change that your team, class or household should adopt. Open with a striking question, a surprising number or a short scene rather than introducing yourself. Give three supporting points and announce each one clearly. End with one sentence that says exactly what you want them to do, let your voice fall on its last word, and hold a moment of silence before you stop.

title: Land your statements
goal: Read a short update aloud with a warm tone mid-sentence and a clear falling note at the end of every statement.
prompt: Read the update aloud as if you were speaking to your team. Keep a light smile in your voice through the middle of each sentence and let the final word of every statement step down in pitch. The last line is a real question, so let that one rise. Leave a short pause before the question.
referenceText: Thanks for joining me this morning. I have gone through the figures in detail. My recommendation is that we launch in March. That gives us six full weeks for testing. I am confident this is the right decision for the team. What questions do you have for me?

title: Recommend one option kindly
goal: Give a clear recommendation between two options while acknowledging the other view warmly and without softeners.
prompt: Your manager asks whether the team should push a project deadline back by two weeks or keep the date and reduce the scope. Give your recommendation in your first sentence, explain one reason, and acknowledge one fair point about the other option in a kind tone. Keep your claims plain, without words like maybe or sort of, and end on a falling note.
